Its contents were not independently retrieved. The saved PDF itself contains Tables 5, 6, A5 and A6 with essay coefficients and standard errors, plus grading procedures and prompts in Appendix B.

paper_design_summary: In proctored laboratory sessions at Middlebury College, students were randomly assigned to permission and access to ChatGPT or a prohibition on generative AI while reading about an unfamiliar technical topic and writing an analytical essay. Approximately one week later they wrote another essay on the same topic without AI or other resources. The paper analyzes ratings of essay quality, linguistic features, and embedding similarity across students and to the assigned reading.

studies.label: Two-session lab experiment: analytical essay with or without generative AI (Session One) and unaided essay one week later (Session Two)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Permission to use generative AI plus a provided ChatGPT account versus a prohibition on generative AI during Session One learning and essay writing. Within each of eight time slots, one of two labs was randomly assigned to each condition, and each student was randomly assigned to a computer in a lab (p. 6, Section 2.1). Topic and the order of the two complementary essay prompts were also randomized (p. 7); Session Two test-versus-essay order was randomized (p. 9). AI assignment is between students; repeated assessments do not make the AI treatment a crossover.
assignment.quote: We randomly assign each student who signed up for a time slot to a specific computer in one of these two labs.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.1, Overview; p. 11, Section 3.3 (time-slot strata); pp. 7 and 9 (other randomizations)
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement for this experiment in the full document; the preregistered study mentioned in Appendix B.7 is another paper.

arms.name: AI-allowed
arms.description: Any generative AI permitted during Session One learning and essay writing, with a dedicated logged-in ChatGPT (GPT-4o) account. Standard online resources are also permitted. All knowledge tests and the Session Two essay prohibit AI (pp. 7-9, 52). Assigned sign-ups: Table 2, p. 36; analyzed Session One students: Table A1, p. 61.

arms.name: AI-forbidden
arms.description: Generative AI prohibited; Google, Wikipedia, the college library website and other standard online resources permitted during Session One learning and essay writing. All knowledge tests and the Session Two essay prohibit AI (pp. 7-9, 52). Assigned sign-ups: Table 2, p. 36; analyzed Session One students: Tables 3-4, pp. 37-38.

participants.exclusions: Table 2 (p. 36) reports 256 assigned sign-ups: 130 AI-allowed and 126 AI-forbidden. Tables 1, 3 and 4 (pp. 35, 37-38) report 211 students analyzed in Session One; 104 analyzed controls are reported in Tables 3-4, and 107 analyzed treated students are printed in Table A1 (p. 61). Table 4 reports 204 analyzed in Session Two, including 102 controls. These study counts are distinct from the essay samples: Table 5 (p. 39) reports Session One linguistic N = 210, control 104, whereas Table A5 (p. 65) reports N = 209, control 104, with identical similarity coefficients. Session Two linguistic N = 199, control 99, in both tables. Table 6 (p. 40) reports quality N = 209, control 104, in Session One and N = 197, control 97, in Session Two. Appendix B.4 (p. 74) skips empty essays and essays with fewer than 20 characters for AI grading. The source does not reconcile the Session One linguistic Ns or provide a complete participant/essay exclusion accounting; the grading rule cannot be assumed to explain all differences.
participants.who: Undergraduates at Middlebury College, recruited campus-wide for 'a study on learning' without mention of AI; mean age 20.1, 35.1 percent male, mean GPA 3.68
participants.quote: the 211 (82.4 percent) who attended Session One (column 2), and the 204 (79.7 percent) who attended both sessions (column 3).
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 3.2; p. 35, Table 1; p. 36, Table 2 (assignment counts); pp. 37-40, Tables 3-6 (analysis counts); pp. 61, 65, Tables A1, A5; p. 74, Appendix B.4

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (GPT-4o), dedicated logged-in account; any generative AI tool permitted (p. 8, Treatment)
ai_tool.how_used: Unrestricted use during the learning phase while reading and producing the Session One essay; no AI permitted for the Session Two essay (pp. 7-9). Account-use assignment effect: 67.3 percentage points, not the treated-arm usage rate (p. 14, Section 4.1; Table 3, p. 37: control mean 0.010, coefficient 0.673, SE 0.046). Conversation logs show explaining concepts for 57 percent of treated students, drafting responses for 31 percent, and summarizing readings for 17 percent (p. 3). The paper reports an assignment effect of 1.9 percentage points on other-model use, not a treated-arm usage rate of about 2 percent (p. 14; Table 3: control mean 0.020, coefficient 0.019, SE 0.024).

task.description: Analytical essay of approximately 500 words on randomly assigned blockchain technology, carbon capture or CRISPR gene editing. Prompts ask students to analyze relationships, compare alternatives and support arguments with evidence. Each student receives one of two complementary prompts in Session One and the other in Session Two (p. 7; Appendix B.2, pp. 69-71). The later essay uses no AI or other resources; its order relative to the knowledge test is randomized (p. 9). This analytical-writing task meets the codebook scope through its comparison of similarity across writers; analytical quality is recorded separately from creativity.
task.duration: Session One: up to 35 minutes for learning and essay writing combined (p. 7). Session Two: up to 20 minutes for the essay, approximately one week later; mean interval 6.99 days (p. 9, Section 2.2 and fn. 5).

outcomes.name: Overall essay quality, Session One (with AI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Holistic overall essay quality on a 0-10 scale, assessing analytical writing rather than originality or creativity. Three or four independent Prolific graders with a master's or PhD rate each essay blind to condition and identity; their scores are averaged within essay, then combined with the AI score for the main human-plus-AI average (pp. 12-13; p. 40, Table 6 notes). The AI grader is Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 as printed (p. 72, Appendix B.4). The measure code is null because the reported outcome averages human and AI scores and the codebook provides no composite-rater code. Its two components correspond to human_raters and automated_score; neither single code identifies the reported composite. The source settles the scoring procedure; an Atlas coding decision is needed for a single measure code. The quality index averages accuracy, evidence, relevance, organization and writing style; this is a robustness measure of quality. Human-only and AI-only ratings are robustness variants (Table A6, p. 66; Figure A4, p. 54). Overall quality is the paper's benchmark measure (p. 71, Appendix B.3). Separate Session One dimension records are omitted under the form's outcome cap; Table 6 Panel A (p. 40) gives assignment coefficients (SE): accuracy 0.198 (0.182), evidence 0.076 (0.223), relevance 0.118 (0.214), organization 0.249 (0.210), writing style 0.202 (0.180).

outcomes.name: Within-group similarity, Session One essays (with AI)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: A student-level score averaging pairwise cosine similarity of that student's essay embedding with all other essays in the same treatment x topic x prompt cell. One essay per student per session. Sentence-embedding model fine-tuned from MPNet; exact checkpoint not stated (p. 13; p. 39, Table 5 notes). Higher similarity means lower diversity; coefficients below retain the paper's similarity sign and would require reversal for the atlas diversity direction. Figures 6 and A5 (pp. 32, 55) show standardized effects and confidence intervals graphically; no numerical values were estimated from the figures.

contrasts.reported: Within-group similarity: control mean 0.774; assignment coefficient (paper column ITT) 0.001 (SE 0.007); TOT 0.001 (SE 0.010). Table 5: N = 210 total, 104 control. Table A5 Panel D repeats the coefficients but prints N = 209 total, 104 control; the correct reconciled outcome N is not established. Section 4.3 calls the effect statistically insignificant and a 0.1 percent change relative to the control mean.
contrasts.locator: p. 39, Table 5, Panel C, cols 1-3; p. 17, Section 4.3; p. 65, Table A5, Panel D; p. 32, Figure 6; p. 55, Figure A5

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of each essay with all other essays in its treatment x topic x prompt cell
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence-embedding model cited to Reimers and Gurevych (2019), fine-tuned from MPNet (Song et al., 2020); exact checkpoint not stated (p. 39, Table 5 notes).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same treatment group, topic and prompt cell (per-student score, then averaged by arm)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Student-level OLS with time-slot strata fixed effects and double-lasso-selected controls; heteroskedasticity-robust SEs. TOT uses two-stage least squares with assignment as instrument (p. 11; Table 5 notes, p. 39). No adjustment is reported for dependence between similarity scores sharing essays, or clustering by lab/time slot.
diversity_detail.notes: AI availability denotes access in the treatment arm, not universal use or access in the control arm. Validation in p. 13, fn. 11: within-topic similarity 0.74 versus 0.15 across topics; same-prompt similarity 0.78 versus 0.71 for the same topic with different prompts.

eligibility.reason: Core eligibility is confirmed after final review. Within each time slot, labs were randomly assigned to AI conditions and individual students were randomly assigned to computers; treatment provided generative-AI access during production of the Session One essay (pp. 6-8, Section 2.1). The study analyzed 211 students in Session One (pp. 37-38, Tables 3-4). The eligible similarity regressions analyzed 210 students according to Table 5 or 209 according to Table A5 in Session One, and 199 in Session Two (pp. 39, 65); all counts are people and exceed 50 without adding sessions or graders. Similarity is computed between each student's essay and other students' essays in the same treatment, topic and prompt cell (p. 13, Section 3.4; p. 39, Table 5 notes). The codebook explicitly includes writing tasks compared across writers for similarity. Session Two essays were produced without AI (p. 9, Section 2.2). The unresolved sample-accounting details and measure-code mappings for ancillary length and quality outcomes do not change any criterion; eligibility rests on the verified diversity outcomes, without treating analytical quality as rated creativity.

one_line_finding: AI access showed no detectable change in between-student essay similarity during access (coefficient 0.001, SE 0.007; control mean 0.774) or one week later without AI (-0.005, SE 0.013; control mean 0.762; p. 39, Table 5 Panel C).
open_questions: The source does not reconcile Session One linguistic N = 210 in Table 5 with N = 209 in Table A5, or fully account for the missing essays in each analysis; the empty/short-essay AI-grading rule only partly documents exclusions.

The paper establishes that S1-O9 and S1-O10 are standardized text-length counts, but the current measure vocabulary has no matching code. Their measure fields are null pending an Atlas coding decision; no additional paper evidence is needed and eligibility is unaffected.

The paper establishes that S1-O3, S1-O4 and S1-O11 through S1-O15 combine human and AI grades, but the current measure vocabulary has no composite-rater code. Their measure fields are null pending an Atlas coding decision; no additional paper evidence is needed and eligibility is unaffected.
notes: Final review covered the entire markdown conversion, including Appendices A-C, and checked the recorded numerical results against the relevant PDF pages. No effect sizes, figure coordinates or unprinted participant counts were computed. The paper labels assignment coefficients ITT, but estimates use attendees and available outcome samples rather than all assigned sign-ups; ITT is retained only as a printed source label. The study-level count of 211 analyzed students in Session One does not apply to every essay outcome. Session Two outcomes compare the original assignment groups. For immediate outcomes, AI availability yes denotes access in the AI-allowed arm; it does not assert universal use. Similarity coefficients retain their printed sign, with higher similarity indicating lower diversity. The paper reports student-level robust SEs without a reported adjustment for shared-essay dependence or lab/time-slot clustering. The unsupported category_count codes for the two length indices and human_raters codes for the seven combined human/AI quality outcomes were replaced with null. Their full scoring procedures and verified statistics are retained. No replacement vocabulary was invented: text-length counts and composite human/AI grades require Atlas coding decisions, not more source evidence. These three challenge problems are counted as corrected because the unsupported assertions were removed; the remaining vocabulary questions are separately recorded as non-eligibility open items. The 15-outcome cap in form-spec.md Rule 7 is retained, with the paper's benchmark overall-quality outcomes first. The array includes both overall-quality outcomes, both within-group similarity outcomes, both lexical-diversity indices, both reading-material similarity outcomes, both length indices, and all five delayed quality dimensions. Separate records for the five immediate quality dimensions and both readability indices remain omitted and disclosed under that cap. The immediate dimension coefficients are preserved in S1-O3 measure_detail (p. 40, Table 6 Panel A); omitted readability indices are in p. 39, Table 5 Panel B, with components in p. 65, Table A5 Panel B. Quality indices, grader-specific ratings and individual lexical/length components are grouped as variants. Academic knowledge tests are not creativity tests; self-reported knowledge, perceptions, Appendix C attitude narratives, AI-detection and plagiarism diagnostics are excluded from creativity outcomes. Usage-subgroup and demographic heterogeneity are analyses of existing outcomes; usage subgroups are defined after assignment. The literature-comparison meta-analysis concerns learning and is not a separate creativity synthesis. No participant overlap, data/code repository or preregistration for this experiment is stated. The external supplement link and its described contents were confirmed from the PDF; the separate file was not retrieved. The unresolved linguistic sample count and complete exclusion accounting require author clarification, with no effect on the eligibility decision. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the historical reconciliation record; the active form and final object record the final decisions.
